**4. Root Cause Analysis**

The root cause analysis was led by Arjun Mehta. The investigation identified two contributing factors that combined to cause the outage.

The postmortem names Arjun Mehta as the root_cause_analysis_lead. Record status: historical.

**4.1 Primary Cause: Connection Pool Exhaustion due to Misconfigured Batch Job**

The batch job `ledger-sync-2024-03-09` was configured to query the payment gateway for the status of all transactions from the previous 48 hours. The job was intended to run with a concurrency of 5 threads. However, a configuration change made on 2024-03-08 incorrectly set the concurrency to 50 threads. This change was not caught by the Finance Automation team's review process. As a result, the job generated a query rate that overwhelmed the database connection pool.

The batch job also lacked a circuit breaker or a rate limiter. When the connection pool began to exhaust, the job retried failed queries aggressively, which compounded the issue.

**4.2 Contributing Cause: Connection Leak in Payment Processing Library**

During the investigation, Arjun Mehta's team discovered a connection leak in the payment processing library `pg-lib` (version 2.4.1). The library was not releasing database connections after completing transactions under certain error conditions. Specifically, when a transaction failed during the callback to the merchant's webhook URL, the library would not return the connection to the pool. This leak was present in the codebase for several months but was not triggered under normal traffic levels.

This appendix provides a summary of the root cause analysis and the associated corrective actions. The information is intended to serve as a reference for the Reliability Operations Team and other stakeholders during the implementation and review of the actions.

### 14.1 Root Cause Analysis Summary

The SEV1 incident on 2024-03-11 was triggered by a combination of factors that, when taken together, led to a cascading failure of the payment gateway service. The primary trigger was a brief power fluctuation in the primary data center (DC-1) at approximately 06:15 IST. This fluctuation caused a momentary loss of power to a subset of the application servers hosting the payment gateway service. The uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems in DC-1 performed as designed, but the transition caused a brief network partition as the servers rebooted.

The failover mechanism, which is designed to redirect traffic to the secondary data center (DC-2), was activated automatically. However, the failover was not clean. The load balancer in DC-2 was configured with a health check interval of 30 seconds. During the failover window, the newly activated instances in DC-2 were still initializing and did not pass the health checks for the first two cycles. This caused the load balancer to mark the service as unhealthy and return HTTP 503 errors to clients for a period of approximately 2 minutes.

The second contributing factor was a pre-existing issue with the connection pool configuration in the payment gateway service. The connection pool size was set to a static value of 50 connections per instance. Under normal traffic conditions, this was sufficient. However, during the failover, the billing service, which is a downstream dependency, experienced a temporary slowdown due to an unrelated batch job that was running at the same time. This caused the connection pool in the payment gateway to become exhausted, leading to additional timeouts and errors.

The combination of the failover delay and the connection pool exhaustion created a cascading effect. The error rate spiked to 12% of all requests, and the service was unable to recover on its own. The on-call engineer was paged at 06:20 IST and manually restarted the affected instances in DC-2 at 06:35 IST. The service returned to normal operation at 06:40 IST.

It is important to note that the power fluctuation was an external event and was not caused by any internal configuration change. However, the failover configuration and the connection pool settings were identified as areas that required improvement to prevent a similar incident in the future.

#### 15.1 Failover Delay Analysis

The automated failover to DC-1 was triggered at 06:18 IST, but the load balancer took approximately 90 seconds to complete the health check cycle for all instances. This delay was longer than the documented 30-second expected failover time. The reason for the delay was traced to the health check interval settings on the load balancer, which had been modified during a previous maintenance window (see Change CHG0029871) without a corresponding update to the runbook. The runbook at the time incorrectly stated the failover time as 30 seconds; this has been corrected in the draft runbook update under CA-02. The actual observed failover time was 90 seconds, which is now reflected in the draft.

#### 15.2 Connection Pool Exhaustion

During the failover window, the connection pool settings on the gateway service were identified as a contributing factor. The maximum pool size was set to 200 connections per instance. During the incident, the number of concurrent requests to the gateway exceeded this limit, causing the pool to become exhausted. Requests waiting for a connection from the pool timed out after 5 seconds. The error rate spike to 12% was directly correlated with this pool exhaustion. The connection pool settings have been flagged for review under CA-04.
#### 15.3 Failover Decision and Impact Assessment

The decision to failover to DC-2 was made at 14:32 IST on 2024-03-11, approximately 90 minutes after the first signs of degradation were observed in DC-1. The primary trigger was the sustained error rate on the payment gateway service, which had crossed the 10% threshold for 15 consecutive minutes. This was in line with the runbook criteria for initiating a failover, though the runbook at the time did not explicitly cover the scenario where the connection pool was already nearing exhaustion.

The failover itself was executed manually rather than through the automated system. The automated failover script was not triggered because the health check on the load balancer still reported the DC-1 instances as healthy. This was later traced to the health check interval modification mentioned in Section 15.1. The decision to proceed manually was taken by the on-call engineer after consulting the incident commander, as the error rate was continuing to climb and the impact on end users was becoming significant.

Impact assessment during the failover window:

- **Transaction loss**: Approximately 2,300 transactions were lost during the 12-minute failover window. These were transactions that had been accepted by the gateway but had not yet been committed to the downstream payment processor. The transactions were not retried automatically, as the retry mechanism was disabled during the incident to prevent duplicate charges. A manual reconciliation process was initiated post-incident under INC-20240312-001 to identify and re-process these transactions. As of the time of this postmortem, 1,850 transactions have been successfully re-processed, with the remaining 450 pending verification with the payment processor.

- **User-facing errors**: The gateway returned HTTP 503 errors to clients during the failover window. The error response included a retry-after header of 30 seconds, which was intended to spread client retry traffic. However, the header value was based on the documented 30-second failover time, which was incorrect. Clients that retried after 30 seconds encountered the ongoing failover and received additional 503 errors. A total of 8,900 unique client requests received at least one 503 response during this period.

- **Database impact**: The db-primary in DC-2 received the full write load immediately after the failover. The database was sized for the normal production load, and the sudden shift caused a brief spike in write latency. The latency peaked at 850 ms per write transaction, compared to the normal 15 ms, for a period of approximately 4 minutes. This was caused by the db-primary having to replay the replication log from DC-1, which had accumulated during the period when the two data centers were out of sync. The db-replica in DC-2 was not promoted to handle reads during this period, as the read replica promotion script had a dependency on the load balancer health check, which was still in the delayed cycle.

- **Cache warming**: The in-memory cache in DC-2 was cold at the time of failover. This caused an increase in cache miss rates, which in turn increased the load on the db-primary. The cache warming process completed approximately 20 minutes after the failover, and the cache hit rate returned to the normal 98% level. During the warming period, the cache hit rate dropped to 72%, and the additional database load was a contributing factor to the write latency spike mentioned above.
## Postmortem - SEV1 Payment Gateway Outage

**Incident ID:** INC-20240312-001  
**Severity:** SEV1  
**Date:** 2024-03-11  
**Service Affected:** payment-gateway-svc  
**Duration:** 13:45 IST to 14:32 IST (47 minutes)  
**Report Date:** 2024-03-16  
**Status:** Approved - pending action item closure

### 1. Executive Summary

On 11 March 2024 at 13:45 IST, the payment-gateway-svc error rate exceeded the 1.5% alerting threshold, triggering a SEV1 incident. The root cause was a misconfiguration in the failover automation that caused a premature switchover to DC-2 while the DC-1 primary database was still serving traffic. The incident lasted 47 minutes and affected approximately 12,400 unique client requests. A total of 8,900 client requests received at least one HTTP 503 response during the failover window. No data loss occurred, though 2,300 transactions required reconciliation.

The incident was declared resolved at 14:32 IST when the error rate returned to baseline. The immediate cause was the failover automation being triggered by a stale health check metric, combined with a documentation error in the runbook that specified an incorrect failover time.

---

### 2. Timeline

All times in IST (UTC+05:30).

| Time | Event |
|------|-------|
| 13:42 | Payment gateway team deploys config change v2.4.1 to increase timeout for upstream bank API from 5s to 8s. |
| 13:45 | Grafana alert fires: payment-gateway-svc error rate above 1.5% (observed 2.1%). On-call engineer acknowledges. |
| 13:47 | Initial investigation begins. Error logs show increased 5xx responses from upstream bank API. |
| 13:52 | On-call engineer checks upstream bank status page - no reported incidents. |
| 13:55 | Error rate climbs to 4.8%. SEV1 declared. Incident commander assigned. |
| 13:58 | Decision made to failover to DC-2. Failover automation initiated. |
| 14:01 | Failover automation completes. Traffic begins routing to DC-2. |
| 14:03 | Error rate drops to 0.8%. Initial assessment suggests failover successful. |
| 14:05 | Error rate rises again to 2.3%. Investigation reveals DC-1 db-primary still receiving writes. |
| 14:08 | Discovery that the failover was premature - DC-1 db-primary was not drained. |
| 14:12 | Decision made to reverse the failover and return traffic to DC-1. |
| 14:15 | Traffic partially returned to DC-1. Error rate fluctuates between 1.2% and 2.7%. |
| 14:18 | db-primary in DC-2 experiences write latency spike (850ms per write). |
| 14:22 | Root cause identified: stale health check metric triggered failover automation prematurely. |
| 14:26 | Manual intervention: failover automation disabled. Traffic fully re-routed to DC-1. |
| 14:29 | Error rate drops to 0.4%. |
| 14:32 | Error rate returns to baseline (<0.1%). Incident declared resolved. |
| 14:35 | Post-incident review meeting scheduled. |

---

### 3. Root Cause Analysis

#### 3.1 Primary Root Cause

The failover automation was triggered by a stale health check metric. The load balancer health check for payment-gateway-svc in DC-1 was configured with a 60-second interval and a 3-failure threshold. However, due to a known bug in the health check agent (tracked as BUG-2210), the health check results were not being refreshed after the agent restarted during a routine maintenance window on 2024-03-11 at 11:30. The agent restarted successfully but did not re-register with the monitoring backend, leaving the last known health status (healthy) frozen in the system.

The incident impacted both the primary API and the webhook notification path. Webhook retries were queued and eventually delivered after the service recovered. Merchant-facing dashboard latency also increased during the incident, though the dashboard remained available.

**3. Timeline Review** (All times IST)

| Time | Event |
|------|-------|
| 13:55 | Batch job `ledger-sync-2024-03-09` launched by the Finance Automation team as part of a scheduled reconciliation run. |
| 14:02 | Batch job begins sending an unusually high volume of transaction status queries to PG-SVC. The query rate is approximately 3x the normal baseline. |
| 14:15 | Database connection pool for PG-SVC reaches 70% utilization. No alert triggered because the pool utilization alert threshold was set to 85%. |
| 14:22 | First 503 errors returned to clients. On-call engineer is paged. |
| 14:28 | On-call engineer acknowledges the page and begins investigating. Initial assumption is a database performance issue. |
| 14:35 | Investigation reveals high connection count on the primary database. The connection pool is at 100% utilization. |
| 14:40 | The on-call engineer attempts to restart the PG-SVC pods, but the connection pool is still saturated by the batch job traffic. |
| 14:45 | Failure rate peaks at 31%. |
| 14:52 | The batch job is identified as the source of the abnormal traffic and is paused by the Finance Automation team. |
| 15:02 | Connection pool is manually scaled from 100 to 300. Pod restart is completed. |
| 15:10 | Error rate begins to decline. |
| 15:38 | Error rate returns to 0%. |
| 16:09 | Incident is declared resolved. Webhook queue backlog is cleared. |

**4. Root Cause Analysis**

The root cause analysis was led by Arjun Mehta. The investigation identified two contributing factors that combined to cause the outage.

The postmortem names Arjun Mehta as the root_cause_analysis_lead. Record status: historical.

**4.1 Primary Cause: Connection Pool Exhaustion due to Misconfigured Batch Job**

The batch job `ledger-sync-2024-03-09` was configured to query the payment gateway for the status of all transactions from the previous 48 hours. The job was intended to run with a concurrency of 5 threads. However, a configuration change made on 2024-03-08 incorrectly set the concurrency to 50 threads. This change was not caught by the Finance Automation team's review process. As a result, the job generated a query rate that overwhelmed the database connection pool.

The batch job also lacked a circuit breaker or a rate limiter. When the connection pool began to exhaust, the job retried failed queries aggressively, which compounded the issue.

**4.2 Contributing Cause: Connection Leak in Payment Processing Library**

During the investigation, Arjun Mehta's team discovered a connection leak in the payment processing library `pg-lib` (version 2.4.1). The library was not releasing database connections after completing transactions under certain error conditions. Specifically, when a transaction failed during the callback to the merchant's webhook URL, the library would not return the connection to the pool. This leak was present in the codebase for several months but was not triggered under normal traffic levels.

## 14. Appendix: Corrective Action Details

This appendix provides a summary of the root cause analysis and the associated corrective actions. The information is intended to serve as a reference for the Reliability Operations Team and other stakeholders during the implementation and review of the actions.

### 14.1 Root Cause Analysis Summary

The SEV1 incident on 2024-03-11 was triggered by a combination of factors that, when taken together, led to a cascading failure of the payment gateway service. The primary trigger was a brief power fluctuation in the primary data center (DC-1) at approximately 06:15 IST. This fluctuation caused a momentary loss of power to a subset of the application servers hosting the payment gateway service. The uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems in DC-1 performed as designed, but the transition caused a brief network partition as the servers rebooted.

The failover mechanism, which is designed to redirect traffic to the secondary data center (DC-2), was activated automatically. However, the failover was not clean. The load balancer in DC-2 was configured with a health check interval of 30 seconds. During the failover window, the newly activated instances in DC-2 were still initializing and did not pass the health checks for the first two cycles. This caused the load balancer to mark the service as unhealthy and return HTTP 503 errors to clients for a period of approximately 2 minutes.

The second contributing factor was a pre-existing issue with the connection pool configuration in the payment gateway service. The connection pool size was set to a static value of 50 connections per instance. Under normal traffic conditions, this was sufficient. However, during the failover, the billing service, which is a downstream dependency, experienced a temporary slowdown due to an unrelated batch job that was running at the same time. This caused the connection pool in the payment gateway to become exhausted, leading to additional timeouts and errors.

The combination of the failover delay and the connection pool exhaustion created a cascading effect. The error rate spiked to 12% of all requests, and the service was unable to recover on its own. The on-call engineer was paged at 06:20 IST and manually restarted the affected instances in DC-2 at 06:35 IST. The service returned to normal operation at 06:40 IST.

It is important to note that the power fluctuation was an external event and was not caused by any internal configuration change. However, the failover configuration and the connection pool settings were identified as areas that required improvement to prevent a similar incident in the future.

### 14.2 Corrective Actions

The following corrective actions have been identified and assigned to the respective teams. The status of each action is tracked in the task tracker and will be reviewed during the weekly reliability meeting.

### 14.3 Notes on Corrective Action Status

- **CA-01**: The Finance Automation Team has communicated the plan for this action. Validation is pending due to the weekend batch window. The team expects to complete the validation by 2024-03-25.
- **CA-02**: The Infrastructure Team has requested access to the deployment runbook repository. The draft of the runbook update is 50% complete. The team is working on the remaining sections.
- **CA-03**: This action has not been started. Rohan Iyer is currently focused on CA-04, which is a higher priority.
- **CA-04**: Rohan Iyer has shared preliminary findings. The leak appears to be related to a missing close call in a specific code path. The investigation is ongoing.
- **CA-05**: The on-call team has started configuring the monitoring alert. The alert configuration is expected to be completed by 2024-03-22.
- **CA-06**: Priya Nair has sent a reminder to the Finance Automation Team about the upcoming training session. The session is scheduled for 2024-03-30.

The following section provides a chronological review of the deployment and hotfix activity surrounding the incident. This timeline is reconstructed from the deployment logs, change management records, and on-call shift notes. #### 15.1 Failover Delay Analysis

The automated failover to DC-1 was triggered at 06:18 IST, but the load balancer took approximately 90 seconds to complete the health check cycle for all instances. This delay was longer than the documented 30-second expected failover time. The reason for the delay was traced to the health check interval settings on the load balancer, which had been modified during a previous maintenance window (see Change CHG0029871) without a corresponding update to the runbook. The runbook at the time incorrectly stated the failover time as 30 seconds; this has been corrected in the draft runbook update under CA-02. The actual observed failover time was 90 seconds, which is now reflected in the draft.

#### 15.2 Connection Pool Exhaustion

During the failover window, the connection pool settings on the gateway service were identified as a contributing factor. The maximum pool size was set to 200 connections per instance. During the incident, the number of concurrent requests to the gateway exceeded this limit, causing the pool to become exhausted. Requests waiting for a connection from the pool timed out after 5 seconds. The error rate spike to 12% was directly correlated with this pool exhaustion. The connection pool settings have been flagged for review under CA-04.

documents.title: Postmortem - SEV1 Payment Gateway Outage
documents.content:
#### 15.3 Failover Decision and Impact Assessment

The decision to failover to DC-2 was made at 14:32 IST on 2024-03-11, approximately 90 minutes after the first signs of degradation were observed in DC-1. The primary trigger was the sustained error rate on the payment gateway service, which had crossed the 10% threshold for 15 consecutive minutes. This was in line with the runbook criteria for initiating a failover, though the runbook at the time did not explicitly cover the scenario where the connection pool was already nearing exhaustion.

The failover itself was executed manually rather than through the automated system. The automated failover script was not triggered because the health check on the load balancer still reported the DC-1 instances as healthy. This was later traced to the health check interval modification mentioned in Section 15.1. The decision to proceed manually was taken by the on-call engineer after consulting the incident commander, as the error rate was continuing to climb and the impact on end users was becoming significant.

Impact assessment during the failover window:

- **Transaction loss**: Approximately 2,300 transactions were lost during the 12-minute failover window. These were transactions that had been accepted by the gateway but had not yet been committed to the downstream payment processor. The transactions were not retried automatically, as the retry mechanism was disabled during the incident to prevent duplicate charges. A manual reconciliation process was initiated post-incident under INC-20240312-001 to identify and re-process these transactions. As of the time of this postmortem, 1,850 transactions have been successfully re-processed, with the remaining 450 pending verification with the payment processor.

- **User-facing errors**: The gateway returned HTTP 503 errors to clients during the failover window. The error response included a retry-after header of 30 seconds, which was intended to spread client retry traffic. However, the header value was based on the documented 30-second failover time, which was incorrect. Clients that retried after 30 seconds encountered the ongoing failover and received additional 503 errors. A total of 8,900 unique client requests received at least one 503 response during this period.

- **Database impact**: The db-primary in DC-2 received the full write load immediately after the failover. The database was sized for the normal production load, and the sudden shift caused a brief spike in write latency. The latency peaked at 850 ms per write transaction, compared to the normal 15 ms, for a period of approximately 4 minutes. This was caused by the db-primary having to replay the replication log from DC-1, which had accumulated during the period when the two data centers were out of sync. The db-replica in DC-2 was not promoted to handle reads during this period, as the read replica promotion script had a dependency on the load balancer health check, which was still in the delayed cycle.

- **Cache warming**: The in-memory cache in DC-2 was cold at the time of failover. This caused an increase in cache miss rates, which in turn increased the load on the db-primary. The cache warming process completed approximately 20 minutes after the failover, and the cache hit rate returned to the normal 98% level. During the warming period, the cache hit rate dropped to 72%, and the additional database load was a contributing factor to the write latency spike mentioned above.

## Postmortem - SEV1 Payment Gateway Outage

**Incident ID:** INC-20240312-001  
**Severity:** SEV1  
**Date:** 2024-03-11  
**Service Affected:** payment-gateway-svc  
**Duration:** 13:45 IST to 14:32 IST (47 minutes)  
**Report Date:** 2024-03-16  
**Status:** Approved - pending action item closure

---

### 1. Executive Summary

On 11 March 2024 at 13:45 IST, the payment-gateway-svc error rate exceeded the 1.5% alerting threshold, triggering a SEV1 incident. The root cause was a misconfiguration in the failover automation that caused a premature switchover to DC-2 while the DC-1 primary database was still serving traffic. The incident lasted 47 minutes and affected approximately 12,400 unique client requests. A total of 8,900 client requests received at least one HTTP 503 response during the failover window. No data loss occurred, though 2,300 transactions required reconciliation.

The incident was declared resolved at 14:32 IST when the error rate returned to baseline. The immediate cause was the failover automation being triggered by a stale health check metric, combined with a documentation error in the runbook that specified an incorrect failover time.

---

### 2. Timeline

All times in IST (UTC+05:30).

| Time | Event |
|------|-------|
| 13:42 | Payment gateway team deploys config change v2.4.1 to increase timeout for upstream bank API from 5s to 8s. |
| 13:45 | Grafana alert fires: payment-gateway-svc error rate above 1.5% (observed 2.1%). On-call engineer acknowledges. |
| 13:47 | Initial investigation begins. Error logs show increased 5xx responses from upstream bank API. |
| 13:52 | On-call engineer checks upstream bank status page - no reported incidents. |
| 13:55 | Error rate climbs to 4.8%. SEV1 declared. Incident commander assigned. |
| 13:58 | Decision made to failover to DC-2. Failover automation initiated. |
| 14:01 | Failover automation completes. Traffic begins routing to DC-2. |
| 14:03 | Error rate drops to 0.8%. Initial assessment suggests failover successful. |
| 14:05 | Error rate rises again to 2.3%. Investigation reveals DC-1 db-primary still receiving writes. |
| 14:08 | Discovery that the failover was premature - DC-1 db-primary was not drained. |
| 14:12 | Decision made to reverse the failover and return traffic to DC-1. |
| 14:15 | Traffic partially returned to DC-1. Error rate fluctuates between 1.2% and 2.7%. |
| 14:18 | db-primary in DC-2 experiences write latency spike (850ms per write). |
| 14:22 | Root cause identified: stale health check metric triggered failover automation prematurely. |
| 14:26 | Manual intervention: failover automation disabled. Traffic fully re-routed to DC-1. |
| 14:29 | Error rate drops to 0.4%. |
| 14:32 | Error rate returns to baseline (<0.1%). Incident declared resolved. |
| 14:35 | Post-incident review meeting scheduled. |

---

### 3. Root Cause Analysis

#### 3.1 Primary Root Cause

The failover automation was triggered by a stale health check metric. The load balancer health check for payment-gateway-svc in DC-1 was configured with a 60-second interval and a 3-failure threshold. However, due to a known bug in the health check agent (tracked as BUG-2210), the health check results were not being refreshed after the agent restarted during a routine maintenance window on 2024-03-11 at 11:30. The agent restarted successfully but did not re-register with the monitoring backend, leaving the last known health status (healthy) frozen in the system.
